newsitem.title: USA: Western firms seek new PPAs for all Hungary plants.
newsitem.headline: Western firms seek new PPAs for all Hungary plants.

text.p: Western firms with stakes in Hungary's ageing power stations said Hungarian energy supplier MVM needed to offer new power purchasing agreements (PPAs) for old as well as new plants.

"We are a little concerned that there a two-tier power generation structure is emerging where you have one tier with a good PPA and another tier with a bad PPA," the U.S. based AES Electric's London-based project development manager Richard Mardon told Reuters on Tuesday.
"It's discriminatory and it's unfair on the existing power stations."

MVM told Reuters earlier that the PPA it had signed with British generator Powergen Plc as a preliminary to a new $261 million power plant in Budapest would serve as model only for new plants and would not apply to existing plants unless they were substantially refurbished.
Three Western utilites have large stakes in existing oil-, gas- and coal-fired plants in Hungary.

A German consortium of RWE Energie AG and EVS operates 800MW of coal-fired capacity at Matra, north-east Hungary, Tractebel of Belgium has oil- ang gas-fired capacity at Dunamenti, in central Hungary, while AES runs three oil- and coal-fired units at its Tisza site, in the east.

All are seeking revised PPAs as they complain that the price they receive for power does not ensure the eight percent profit margin all foreign investors were promised when they bought into the sector in 1995 and 1996.

"We don't want to change the PPA with the existing power stations," MVM's strategic director Istvan Bakacs told Reuters earlier, adding that an exception could be made in the case of "major refurbishments."
Mardon said AES would regret any decision to exclude old plants from new negotations on the price MVM pays for electricity.

"We would be pressing for a renegotiation of the PPA for all power stations to have a level playing field and there is no reason why the Powergen PPA cannot be applied to the industry as a whole," he said.
Tractebel's representative in Hungary Tibor Kuhl also said the new power pricing system should not discriminate between old and new power stations. Only plants soon to be wound down could be exempt.

"A power plant which has been put into service last year or the year before should have the same PPA as for a power plant under negotiation today because the new system should not make any discrimination beween existing and old," he told Reuters.
"But I would accept that with very old power plants which should be decommissioned over two or three years there is no need to renegotiate PPAs."
MVM said on Monday it planned to invite two tenders in July for the construction of 2000 megawatts of new Hungarian capacity.
The first tender will be for smaller capacity units of 20 to 200 MW for commissioning beween 2001 and 2003 while the second will be for larger plants to go on line between 2003 and 2005.
Mardon told Reuters he expected all three of AES's interests in Hungary to enter the tenders.
